claim: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a prevalent systemic autoimmune disease, caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
source: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a prevalent systemic autoimmune disease, caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about RA etiology.

claim: Animal models suggest a role for intestinal bacteria in supporting the systemic immune response required for joint inflammation.
source: Animal models suggest a role for intestinal bacteria in supporting the systemic immune response required for joint inflammation.
evidence: This claim references findings from animal model studies, which are cited works in the field.

claim: 16S sequencing was performed on 114 stool samples from rheumatoid arthritis patients and controls.
source: Here we performed 16S sequencing on 114 stool samples from rheumatoid arthritis patients and controls
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Shotgun sequencing was performed on a subset of 44 samples.
source: shotgun sequencing on a subset of 44 such samples
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The presence of Prevotella copri is strongly correlated with disease in new-onset untreated rheumatoid arthritis (NORA) patients.
source: We identified the presence of Prevotella copri as strongly correlated with disease in new-onset untreated rheumatoid arthritis (NORA) patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 16S and shotgun sequencing data analysis.

claim: Increases in Prevotella abundance correlated with a reduction in Bacteroides in NORA subjects.
source: Increases in Prevotella abundance correlated with a reduction in Bacteroides and a loss of reportedly beneficial microbes in NORA subjects.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the microbiome sequencing data.

claim: Increases in Prevotella abundance correlated with a loss of reportedly beneficial microbes in NORA subjects.
source: Increases in Prevotella abundance correlated with a reduction in Bacteroides and a loss of reportedly beneficial microbes in NORA subjects.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the microbiome sequencing data and references to literature on beneficial microbes.

claim: Unique Prevotella genes were identified that correlated with disease.
source: We also identified unique Prevotella genes that correlated with disease.
evidence: This is based on metagenomic analysis comparing NORA and healthy samples.

claim: Colonization of mice with P. copri resulted in the ability of P. copri to dominate the intestinal microbiota.
source: Further, colonization of mice revealed the ability of P. copri to dominate the intestinal microbiota
evidence: This is based on experimental mouse colonization studies.

claim: Colonization of mice with P. copri resulted in an increased sensitivity to chemically induced colitis.
source: colonization of mice revealed the ability of P. copri to dominate the intestinal microbiota and resulted in an increased sensitivity to chemically induced colitis
evidence: This is based on experimental DSS-induced colitis studies in mice.

claim: P. copri has a potential role in the pathogenesis of RA.
source: This work identifies a potential role for P. copri in the pathogenesis of RA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined human and mouse experimental data.

claim: If left untreated, RA can lead to chronic joint deformity, disability, and increased mortality.
source: If left untreated, RA can lead to chronic joint deformity, disability, and increased mortality.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about RA outcomes.

claim: Many genetic susceptibility risk alleles for RA have been discovered and validated.
source: Many genetic susceptibility risk alleles have been discovered and validated (Stahl et al., 2010)
evidence: This references published genetic studies.

claim: Genetic risk alleles are insufficient to explain RA disease incidence.
source: Many genetic susceptibility risk alleles have been discovered and validated (Stahl et al., 2010) but are insufficient to explain disease incidence.
evidence: This is an inference from genetic studies showing incomplete penetrance.

claim: RA is a complex (multifactorial) disease requiring both environmental and genetic factors for onset.
source: RA is therefore a complex (multifactorial) disease requiring both environmental and genetic factors for onset (Mcinnes and Schett, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited review.

claim: The intestinal microbiota has emerged as a possible environmental factor responsible for the priming of aberrant systemic immunity in RA.
source: Among environmental factors, the intestinal microbiota has emerged as a possible candidate responsible for the priming of aberrant systemic immunity in RA (Scher and Abramson, 2011).
evidence: This is based on a cited review of the field.

claim: The microbiota encompasses hundreds of bacterial species whose products represent an enormous antigenic burden.
source: The microbiota encompasses hundreds of bacterial species whose products represent an enormous antigenic burden that must largely be compartmentalized to prevent immune system activation (Littman and Pamer, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited review.

claim: In RA, there is increased production of both self-reactive antibodies and pro-inflammatory T lymphocytes.
source: In RA, there is increased production of both self-reactive antibodies and pro-inflammatory T lymphocytes.
evidence: This is established clinical and immunological knowledge about RA.

claim: Studies in animal models suggest that both T cell and antibody responses are involved in arthritogenesis.
source: Although mechanisms for targeting of synovium by inflammatory cells have not been fully elucidated, studies in animal models suggest that both T cell and antibody responses are involved in arthritogenesis.
evidence: This references findings from animal model studies.

claim: An imbalance in the composition of the gut microbiota can alter local T-cell responses and modulate systemic inflammation.
source: Moreover, an imbalance in the composition of the gut microbiota can alter local T-cell responses and modulate systemic inflammation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from microbiome research.

claim: Germ-free mice lack pro-inflammatory Th17 cells.
source: Mice rendered deficient for the microbiota (germ-free) lack pro-inflammatory Th17 cells
evidence: This is based on cited experimental studies.

claim: Colonization of the gastrointestinal tract with segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB) is sufficient to induce accumulation of Th17 cells in the lamina propria.
source: colonization of the gastrointestinal tract with segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB), a commensal microbe commonly found in mammals, is sufficient to induce accumulation of Th17 cells in the lamina propria (Ivanov et al., 2009; Sczesnak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental studies.

claim: In several animal models of arthritis, mice are persistently healthy when raised in germ-free conditions.
source: In several animal models of arthritis, mice are persistently healthy when raised in germ-free conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge from animal model studies.

claim: The introduction of specific gut bacterial species is sufficient to induce joint inflammation in germ-free mice.
source: However, the introduction of specific gut bacterial species is sufficient to induce joint inflammation (Rath et al., 1996; Abdollahi-Roodsaz et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2010)
evidence: This is based on cited experimental studies.

claim: Antibiotic treatment both prevents and abrogates a rheumatoid arthritis-like phenotype in several mouse models.
source: antibiotic treatment both prevents and abrogates a rheumatoid arthritis-like phenotype in several mouse models
evidence: This is established knowledge from animal model studies.

claim: Upon mono-colonization of arthritis-prone K/BxN mice with SFB, the induced Th17 cells potentiate inflammatory disease.
source: Upon mono-colonization of arthritis-prone K/BxN mice with SFB, the induced Th17 cells potentiate inflammatory disease (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on a cited experimental study.

claim: An imbalance in intestinal microbial ecology, in which SFB is dominant, may result in reduced proportions or functions of anti-inflammatory regulatory T cells (Treg).
source: An imbalance in intestinal microbial ecology, in which SFB is dominant, may result in reduced proportions or functions of anti-inflammatory regulatory T cells (Treg) and a predisposition towards autoimmunity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cited and discussed studies.

claim: Microbial imbalance may result in a predisposition towards autoimmunity.
source: An imbalance in intestinal microbial ecology, in which SFB is dominant, may result in reduced proportions or functions of anti-inflammatory regulatory T cells (Treg) and a predisposition towards autoimmunity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cited and discussed studies.

claim: Microbial effects appear to affect not only the local immune response, but also systemic inflammatory processes.
source: This appears to affect not only the local immune response, but also systemic inflammatory processes
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies.

claim: Microbial effects may explain, at least in part, reduced Treg cell function in RA patients.
source: may explain, at least in part, reduced Treg cell function in RA patients (Zanin-Zhorov et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting microbiome effects to a cited clinical observation.

claim: T cells whose functions are dictated by intestinal commensal bacteria can be effectors of pathogenesis in tissue-specific autoimmune disease.
source: Thus, T cells whose functions are dictated by intestinal commensal bacteria can be effectors of pathogenesis in tissue-specific autoimmune disease.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited animal model studies.

claim: Recent studies of the human microbiome have characterized the composition and diversity of the healthy gut microbiome.
source: Although recent studies of the human microbiome (Arumugam et al., 2011; Human Microbiome Project Consortium, 2012) have characterized the composition and diversity of the healthy gut microbiome
evidence: This references published microbiome studies.

claim: Disease-associated studies revealed correlations between taxonomic abundance and some clinical phenotypes.
source: disease-associated studies revealed correlations between taxonomic abundance and some clinical phenotypes (Frank et al., 2011; Morgan et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2012)
evidence: This references published disease-microbiome association studies.

claim: A role for distinct microbial taxa and metagenomic markers in systemic inflammatory disease has not been defined.
source: a role for distinct microbial taxa and metagenomic markers in systemic inflammatory disease has not been defined
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Treatment with antibiotics has been a therapeutic modality in RA for decades.
source: While treatment with antibiotics has been a therapeutic modality in RA for decades
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: No microbial organism has been shown to be associated with RA prior to this study.
source: no microbial organism has been shown to be associated with the disease
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: SFB-induced Th17 cells directly contribute to the onset of arthritis in gnotobiotic mice.
source: Based on the discovery that SFB-induced Th17 cells directly contribute to the onset of arthritis in gnotobiotic mice (Wu et al., 2010)
evidence: This references a cited experimental study.

claim: The study analyzed the fecal microbiota in patients with RA using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing.
source: we analyzed the fecal microbiota in patients with RA. We used 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing to classify the microbiota
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The study included patients with new-onset (untreated) RA, chronic (treated) RA, psoriatic arthritis, and age- and ethnicity-matched healthy controls.
source: We used 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing to classify the microbiota in patients with new-onset (untreated) RA, chronic (treated) RA, psoriatic arthritis, and age- and ethnicity-matched healthy controls.
evidence: This describes the study cohorts.

claim: A marked association of Prevotella copri with new-onset RA (NORA) patients was found.
source: We found a marked association of Prevotella copri with new-onset RA (NORA) patients and not with other patient groups.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 16S sequencing data analysis.

claim: Prevotella copri was not associated with other patient groups (chronic RA, psoriatic arthritis, healthy controls).
source: We found a marked association of Prevotella copri with new-onset RA (NORA) patients and not with other patient groups.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 16S sequencing data analysis.

claim: Shotgun sequencing of the microbiome indicated that some P. copri genes are differentially present in NORA-associated and healthy samples.
source: Shotgun sequencing of the microbiome indicated that some P. copri genes are differentially present in NORA-associated and healthy samples.
evidence: This is based on metagenomic analysis.

claim: Colonization of mice with P. copri enhanced susceptibility to chemical colitis.
source: Colonization of mice with P. copri enhanced susceptibility to chemical colitis
evidence: This is based on experimental DSS-induced colitis studies in mice.

claim: Enhanced susceptibility to colitis is consistent with a pro-inflammatory potential of P. copri.
source: Colonization of mice with P. copri enhanced susceptibility to chemical colitis, consistent with a pro-inflammatory potential of this organism.
evidence: This is an inference from the mouse colitis data.

claim: NORA-associated P. copri may contribute to the pathogenesis of human arthritis.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that NORA-associated P. copri may contribute to the pathogenesis of human arthritis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined human and mouse experimental data.

claim: 44 samples were collected from NORA patients at time of initial diagnosis and prior to immunosuppressive treatment.
source: 44 samples collected from NORA patients at time of initial diagnosis and prior to immunosuppressive treatment
evidence: This describes the study cohort.

claim: 26 samples were collected from patients with chronic, treated rheumatoid arthritis (CRA).
source: 26 samples from patients with chronic, treated rheumatoid arthritis (CRA)
evidence: This describes the study cohort.

claim: 16 samples were collected from patients with psoriatic arthritis (PsA).
source: 16 samples from patients with psoriatic arthritis (PsA)
evidence: This describes the study cohort.

claim: 28 samples were collected from healthy controls (HLT).
source: 28 samples from healthy controls (HLT)
evidence: This describes the study cohort.

claim: PsA patients revealed a reduction in sample diversity similar to that of IBD patients.
source: Although PsA patients revealed a reduction in sample diversity similar to that of IBD patients (Morgan et al., 2012)
evidence: This is based on analysis of diversity metrics and comparison to a cited study.

claim: Diversity was comparable between NORA, CRA and healthy groups at 3.02 +/− 0.66 (mean, SD) overall by Shannon Diversity Index.
source: diversity was comparable between NORA, CRA and healthy groups at 3.02 +/− 0.66 (mean, SD) overall by Shannon Diversity Index (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on calculation of Shannon Diversity Index from the sequencing data.

claim: When applying Simpson's Dominance Index, the NORA group was less diverse.
source: However, when applying Simpson's Dominance Index, the NORA group was less diverse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is based on calculation of Simpson's Dominance Index from the sequencing data.

claim: NORA patients harbored a relatively higher abundance of common taxa.
source: suggesting that these patients harbored a relatively higher abundance of common taxa
evidence: This is an inference from the Simpson's Dominance Index results.

claim: Analysis at the major taxonomic hierarchy levels showed no significant differences in either phyla abundance or the ratio of Bacteroidetes/Firmicutes between all groups.
source: Analysis at the major taxonomic hierarchy levels showed no significant differences in either phyla abundance or the ratio of Bacteroidetes/Firmicutes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) between all groups.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of phyla-level abundances.

claim: At the level of family abundances, there was a significant enrichment of Prevotellaceae in NORA subjects.
source: At the level of family abundances, however, we noted a significant enrichment of Prevotellaceae in NORA subjects (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of family-level abundances.

claim: LEfSe analysis found a positive association of two specific Prevotella OTUs with NORA.
source: Using the linear discriminant effect size method (LEfSe, see 'Materials and methods') (Segata et al., 2011) to compare detected clades (33 families, 177 genera, 996 OTUs) among all groups, we found a positive association of two specific Prevotella OTUs with NORA
evidence: This is based on LEfSe statistical analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: LEfSe analysis found an inverse correlation of NORA with Group XIV Clostridia, Lachnospiraceae, and Bacteroides as compared to healthy controls.
source: we found a positive association of two specific Prevotella OTUs with NORA and an inverse correlation with Group XIV Clostridia, Lachnospiraceae, and Bacteroides as compared to healthy controls (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on LEfSe statistical analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: OTU4 was the most highly represented Prevotellaceae OTU with 171,486 supporting reads at 11.49 +/− 17.85 (mean, SD) percent of reads per sample.
source: Of all detected Prevotellaceae OTUs, OTU4 was the most highly represented with 171,486 supporting reads at 11.49 +/− 17.85 (mean, SD) percent of reads per sample.
evidence: This is based on quantification of sequencing reads.

claim: OTU12 was the next most abundant Prevotellaceae, supported by 12,119 reads at 2.00 +/− 5.42 (mean, SD) percent of reads per sample.
source: OTU12, the next most abundant Prevotellaceae, was supported by 12,119 reads at 2.00 +/− 5.42 (mean, SD) percent of reads per sample.
evidence: This is based on quantification of sequencing reads.

claim: Other Prevotellaceae OTUs (including Prevotella OTU934) were more scarcely represented with 1,232 +/− 2,305 (mean, SD) total supporting reads at less than 0.5% total reads per sample.
source: Other Prevotellaceae OTUs (including Prevotella OTU934) were more scarcely represented with 1,232 +/− 2,305 (mean, SD) total supporting reads at less than 0.5% total reads per sample.
evidence: This is based on quantification of sequencing reads.

claim: OTU4 was the dominant Prevotella in the cohort with sixfold more supporting reads than the next most abundant OTU.
source: We therefore reasoned that OTU4 was the dominant Prevotella in our cohort with sixfold more supporting reads than the next most abundant OTU.
evidence: This is an inference from the read count data.

claim: Principal coordinate analysis with Bray-Curtis distances demonstrated that subjects form distinct clusters, irrespective of health or disease status.
source: Principal coordinate analysis with Bray-Curtis distances demonstrated that subjects form distinct clusters, irrespective of health or disease status (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on PCoA analysis of the microbiome data.

claim: The largest component of microbial variation corresponded to the carriage (or absence) of Prevotella.
source: The largest component of microbial variation corresponded to the carriage (or absence) of Prevotella
evidence: This is an inference from the PCoA analysis.

claim: Prevotella carriage significantly differentiated NORA subjects from healthy controls and other forms of arthritis.
source: which significantly differentiated NORA subjects from healthy controls and other forms of arthritis
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the PCoA results.

claim: There is segregation of Prevotella or Bacteroides dominance in the intestinal microbiome.
source: Consistent with other reports of either high Prevotella or high Bacteroides relative abundance, but rarely a high relative abundance of both, (Faust et al., 2012; Yatsunenko et al., 2012), we found segregation of Prevotella or Bacteroides dominance in the intestinal microbiome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the microbiome data and comparison to cited studies.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis revealed Prevotella OTU4, OTU12, and OTU934 to cluster tightly with Prevotella copri.
source: The analysis revealed these OTUs to cluster tightly with Prevotella copri, a microbe isolated from human feces (Hayashi et al., 2007) and sequenced as part of the HMP's reference genome initiative.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic tree construction from 16S sequences.

claim: Four high abundance NORA samples (028B, 030B, 061B, and 089B) were selected for shotgun sequencing.
source: To further characterize Prevotella OTU4, the most abundant taxon, we selected four high abundance NORA samples (028B, 030B, 061B, and 089B) for shotgun sequencing (single-end, 454 platform).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: PhyloPhlAn analysis produced a phylogenomic tree placing the taxon most represented in each sample's metagenomic contigs in close association with Prevotella copri.
source: This produced a phylogenomic tree placing the taxon most represented in each sample's metagenomic contigs (i.e., Prevotella OTU4) again in close association with Prevotella copri (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on PhyloPhlAn phylogenomic analysis of metagenomic assemblies.

claim: Comparison of draft patient-derived P. copri assemblies to reference P. copri and to one another revealed a high degree of similarity, with possible genome rearrangements.
source: Comparison of these draft assemblies to reference P. copri and to one another revealed a high degree of similarity, with possible genome rearrangements (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on genome alignment analysis.

claim: 75% (33/44) of NORA patients carried P. copri in their intestinal microbiota at a threshold for presence of >5% relative abundance.
source: Overall, 75% (33/44) of NORA patients and 21.4% (6/28) of healthy controls carried P. copri in their intestinal microbiota compared to 11.5% (3/26) and 37.5% (6/16) in CRA and PsA patients, respectively, at a threshold for presence of >5% relative abundance.
evidence: This is based on quantification of P. copri abundance from sequencing data.

claim: 21.4% (6/28) of healthy controls carried P. copri in their intestinal microbiota at a threshold for presence of >5% relative abundance.
source: Overall, 75% (33/44) of NORA patients and 21.4% (6/28) of healthy controls carried P. copri in their intestinal microbiota compared to 11.5% (3/26) and 37.5% (6/16) in CRA and PsA patients, respectively, at a threshold for presence of >5% relative abundance.
evidence: This is based on quantification of P. copri abundance from sequencing data.

claim: 11.5% (3/26) of CRA patients carried P. copri in their intestinal microbiota at a threshold for presence of >5% relative abundance.
source: Overall, 75% (33/44) of NORA patients and 21.4% (6/28) of healthy controls carried P. copri in their intestinal microbiota compared to 11.5% (3/26) and 37.5% (6/16) in CRA and PsA patients, respectively, at a threshold for presence of >5% relative abundance.
evidence: This is based on quantification of P. copri abundance from sequencing data.

claim: 37.5% (6/16) of PsA patients carried P. copri in their intestinal microbiota at a threshold for presence of >5% relative abundance.
source: Overall, 75% (33/44) of NORA patients and 21.4% (6/28) of healthy controls carried P. copri in their intestinal microbiota compared to 11.5% (3/26) and 37.5% (6/16) in CRA and PsA patients, respectively, at a threshold for presence of >5% relative abundance.
evidence: This is based on quantification of P. copri abundance from sequencing data.

claim: The prevalence of P. copri in NORA compared to CRA, PsA, and healthy controls was statistically significant by chi-squared test.
source: The prevalence of P. copri in NORA compared to CRA, PsA, and healthy controls was statistically significant by chi-squared test
evidence: This is based on chi-squared statistical test of prevalence data.

claim: The prevalence of P. copri was not significant in pairwise comparisons of CRA, PsA, and healthy controls.
source: but was not significant in pairwise comparisons of the latter three cohorts (Table 3)
evidence: This is based on pairwise statistical comparisons.

claim: Initial shotgun sequencing of the patient-derived strains showed their similarity to P. copri.
source: Although initial shotgun sequencing of the patient-derived strains showed their similarity to P. copri
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: There were notable differences observed in assembled genomes upon comparison with the P. copri reference genome.
source: there were notable differences observed in assembled genomes upon comparison with the P. copri reference genome
evidence: This is based on genome comparison analysis.

claim: The presence or absence of particular genes in P. copri strains might correlate with health or disease phenotypes in this cohort.
source: This observation suggested that the presence or absence of particular genes in these strains might correlate with health or disease phenotypes in this cohort.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed genomic differences.

claim: Shotgun sequencing was performed on fecal DNA from NORA and healthy subjects to compare Prevotella sequences.
source: To address this question, we performed shotgun sequencing on fecal DNA from NORA and healthy subjects
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Prevotella sequences from 18 NORA Prevotella-positive subjects were compared to those of P. copri from 17 healthy subjects.
source: chose to compare Prevotella sequences from 18 NORA Prevotella-positive subjects, which allowed for a depth of at least 7 M Prevotella-aligned reads (paired-end, 100 nt, Illumina platform), to those of P. copri from 17 healthy subjects (including 15 from the HMP database and 2 HLT from our cohort) (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and sample selection.

claim: Overall coverage of the P. copri reference genome was similar between healthy and NORA subjects in all but a few regions.
source: Overall, coverage was similar between healthy and NORA subjects in all but a few regions (Figure 3A, blue and red horizontal lines).
evidence: This is based on genome coverage analysis.

claim: Eight regions were poorly covered in all subjects with mean coverage below the 25th percentile of 0.79 FPKM.
source: Eight regions were poorly covered in all subjects with mean coverage below the 25th percentile of 0.79 FPKM
evidence: This is based on genome coverage analysis.

claim: Several regions showed substantial variability between individuals.
source: while several regions showed substantial variability between individuals (Figure 3A, gray vertical lines)
evidence: This is based on genome coverage analysis.

claim: Carriage of P. copri genes within an individual varied little between samplings.
source: In concordance with a previous report (Schloissnig et al., 2013) documenting the temporal stability of metagenomic SNP patterns in individuals, we found that carriage of P. copri genes within an individual varied little between samplings.
evidence: This is based on MetaPhlAn analysis of HMP longitudinal samples and comparison to a cited study.

claim: A stable set of P. copri core marker genes is common to all samples.
source: In addition to a stable set of P. copri core marker genes common to all samples
evidence: This is based on MetaPhlAn marker gene analysis.

claim: A subset of variable marker genes was observed to co-occur in islands across the P. copri genome.
source: a subset of variable marker genes was observed to co-occur in islands across the P. copri genome
evidence: This is based on MetaPhlAn marker gene analysis.

claim: Co-occurrence of variable marker genes in islands suggests genomic rearrangements as a mechanism of variability.
source: suggesting genomic rearrangements as a mechanism of variability (Figure 3A, blue boxes below plot)
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of variable marker genes.

claim: P. copri strains vary between individuals and retain their individuality over time.
source: Together, these results suggest that P. copri strains vary between individuals and retain their individuality over time.
evidence: This is an inference from the genome coverage and marker gene stability analyses.

claim: Two ORFs were found to be differentially present in healthy controls.
source: We found two ORFs differentially present in healthy controls, and 17 ORFs differentially present in NORA (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ORF presence/absence.

claim: 17 ORFs were found to be differentially present in NORA.
source: We found two ORFs differentially present in healthy controls, and 17 ORFs differentially present in NORA (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ORF presence/absence.

claim: The two healthy-specific ORFs appear on the same metagenomic contig, encoding a nearly-complete nuo operon for NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase.
source: The two healthy-specific ORFs appear on the same metagenomic contig, encoding a nearly-complete nuo operon for NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and contig analysis.

claim: The nuo operon is adjacent to a Bacteroides conjugative transposon.
source: adjacent to a Bacteroides conjugative transposon
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and contig analysis.

claim: Two of the NORA-specific ORFs appear together on another metagenomic contig, encoding an ATP-binding cassette iron transporter.
source: Similarly, two of the NORA-specific ORFs appear together on another metagenomic contig, encoding an ATP-binding cassette iron transporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and contig analysis.

claim: These ORFs may represent good biomarkers for discrimination between healthy and disease-associated microbiota in the population at risk for RA.
source: These ORFs may represent good biomarkers for discrimination between healthy and disease-associated microbiota in the population at risk for RA.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential diagnostic utility of the identified ORFs.

claim: HUMAnN was applied to quantitate the coverage and abundances of KEGG modules in healthy controls (n = 5) and NORA subjects (n = 14).
source: To determine if the NORA metagenome encodes unique functions compared to healthy subjects, we applied HUMAnN (Abubucker et al., 2012) to quantitate the coverage and abundances of KEGG (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000) modules (small sets of genes in well-defined metabolic pathways) in healthy controls (n = 5) and a representative set of NORA subjects (n = 14) with and without Prevotella.
evidence: This describes the functional metagenomic analysis methodology.

claim: Analysis revealed a low abundance of vitamin metabolism (i.e., biotin, pyroxidal, and folate) modules in NORA.
source: This analysis revealed a low abundance of vitamin metabolism (i.e., biotin, pyroxidal, and folate) and pentose phosphate pathway modules in NORA
evidence: This is based on HUMAnN and LEfSe analysis of metagenomic data.

claim: Analysis revealed a low abundance of pentose phosphate pathway modules in NORA.
source: This analysis revealed a low abundance of vitamin metabolism (i.e., biotin, pyroxidal, and folate) and pentose phosphate pathway modules in NORA
evidence: This is based on HUMAnN and LEfSe analysis of metagenomic data.

claim: The low abundance of vitamin metabolism and pentose phosphate pathway modules is consistent with a lack of these functions in Prevotella genomes.
source: consistent with a lack of these functions in Prevotella genomes (Figure 4)
evidence: This is an inference connecting the metagenomic findings to known Prevotella genomic features.

claim: At the coverage level, the NORA metagenome is defined by an absence of functions present in Bacteroides and Clostridia.
source: At the coverage level (presence or absence), the NORA metagenome is defined by an absence of functions present in Bacteroides and Clostridia, clades typically found in low abundance in Prevotella-high NORA subjects.
evidence: This is based on HUMAnN analysis of metagenomic data.

claim: Prevotella and Bacteroides are closely related both functionally and phylogenetically.
source: Prevotella and Bacteroides are closely related both functionally and phylogenetically
evidence: This is established knowledge from microbial taxonomy and genomics.

claim: Prevotella and Bacteroides are rarely found together in high relative abundance despite their ability to dominate the gut microbiome individually.
source: yet, surprisingly, are rarely found together in high relative abundance despite their ability to dominate the gut microbiome individually (Faust et al., 2012)
evidence: This is based on a cited study and observations from this study.

claim: There might be a genetic difference in Prevotella and Bacteroides that could account for their apparent co-exclusionary relationship.
source: We hypothesized that there might be a genetic difference in these two clades that could account for their apparent co-exclusionary relationship.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: K05919 (superoxide reductase) is uniquely present in P. copri but not in any of the most abundant Bacteroides species.
source: This revealed K05919 (superoxide reductase), K00390 (phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase), and several transporters as uniquely present in P. copri (Supplementary file 1C)
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: K00390 (phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase) is uniquely present in P. copri but not in any of the most abundant Bacteroides species.
source: This revealed K05919 (superoxide reductase), K00390 (phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase), and several transporters as uniquely present in P. copri (Supplementary file 1C)
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Several transporters are uniquely present in P. copri but not in any of the most abundant Bacteroides species.
source: This revealed K05919 (superoxide reductase), K00390 (phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase), and several transporters as uniquely present in P. copri (Supplementary file 1C)
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: A set of genes is absent in P. copri but present in Bacteroides.
source: and also a set of genes absent in P. copri but present in Bacteroides (Supplementary file 1D)
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Certain alleles within the human leukocyte-antigen (HLA) Class II locus confer higher risk of RA disease.
source: Certain alleles within the human leukocyte-antigen (HLA) Class II locus confer higher risk of disease, in particular those belonging to DRB1 (i.e., 'shared epitope' alleles or SE) (du Montcel et al., 2005; Gregersen et al., 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited genetic studies.

claim: HLA sequencing was carried out on DNA from all participants in the study.
source: To determine whether a higher abundance of P. copri is associated with the host genotype, we carried out HLA sequencing on DNA from all participants in our study (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The presence of SE alleles correlated with the composition of the gut microbiota.
source: Consistent with recently published mouse data (Gomez et al., 2012), the presence of SE alleles correlated with the composition of the gut microbiota.
evidence: This is based on analysis of HLA genotype and microbiome data, and comparison to a cited mouse study.

claim: A subgroup analysis of NORA patients and healthy controls according to presence (or absence) of SE alleles revealed a significantly higher relative abundance of P. copri in those subjects lacking predisposing genes.
source: A subgroup analysis of NORA patients and healthy controls according to presence (or absence) of SE alleles revealed a significantly higher relative abundance of P. copri in those subjects lacking predisposing genes (Figure 5, p<0.001 in NORA, p<0.05 in HLT, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of P. copri abundance stratified by SE allele status.

claim: Antibiotic-treated C57BL/6 mice were colonized with P. copri by oral gavage.
source: To determine if the Prevotella-associated metagenome is sufficient to predispose to increased inflammatory responses, antibiotic-treated C57BL/6 mice were colonized with P. copri by oral gavage.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Analysis of DNA extracted from fecal samples 2 weeks post-gavage revealed robust colonization with P. copri.
source: Analysis of DNA extracted from fecal samples 2 weeks post-gavage revealed robust colonization with P. copri (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on qPCR analysis of fecal DNA.

claim: Sequencing of the 16S gene in fecal DNA from two representative mice colonized with P. copri revealed the ability of Prevotella to dominate the gut microbiota.
source: Sequencing of the 16S gene (regions V1–V2, 454 platform) in fecal DNA from two representative mice colonized with P. copri revealed the ability of Prevotella to dominate the gut microbiota (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on 16S sequencing analysis of mouse fecal samples.

claim: P. copri-colonized mice had reduced Bacteroidales and Lachnospiraceae compared to mice gavaged with media alone.
source: In comparison to fecal DNA from mice gavaged with media alone, P. copri-colonized mice had reduced Bacteroidales and Lachnospiraceae, similar to what was observed in this patient cohort (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on 16S sequencing analysis of mouse fecal samples.

claim: Exposure of P. copri-colonized mice to 2% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) in drinking water for 7 days resulted in more severe colitis as assessed by enhanced weight loss.
source: Consistent with a previous report of a Prevotella taxon exacerbating an inflammatory phenotype (Elinav et al., 2011), exposure of P. copri-colonized mice to 2% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) in drinking water for 7 days resulted in more severe colitis as assessed by enhanced weight loss (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is based on experimental DSS-induced colitis studies in mice and comparison to a cited study.

claim: Exposure of P. copri-colonized mice to DSS resulted in more severe colitis as assessed by worse endoscopic score.
source: resulted in more severe colitis as assessed by enhanced weight loss (Figure 6C), worse endoscopic score (Figure 6D)
evidence: This is based on experimental DSS-induced colitis studies in mice.

claim: Exposure of P. copri-colonized mice to DSS resulted in more severe colitis as assessed by increased epithelial damage on histological analysis.
source: resulted in more severe colitis as assessed by enhanced weight loss (Figure 6C), worse endoscopic score (Figure 6D), and increased epithelial damage on histological analysis (Figure 6E,F) when compared to littermate controls gavaged with media alone.
evidence: This is based on experimental DSS-induced colitis studies in mice.

claim: P. copri colonized mice showed significantly decreased weight loss at day 7 following DSS exposure compared to mice colonized with Bacteroides thetaiotamicron.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to mice colonized with mouse commensal Bacteroides thetaiotamicron (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), P. copri colonized mice similarly showed significantly decreased weight loss at day 7 following DSS exposure (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on experimental DSS-induced colitis studies comparing P. copri and B. thetaiotamicron colonization.

claim: Analysis of the lamina propria CD4+ T-cell response revealed an increase in IFNγ production following DSS induction.
source: Analysis of the lamina propria CD4+ T-cell response revealed an increase in IFNγ production following DSS induction
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry analysis of lamina propria T cells.

claim: No statistically significant differences were seen in IFNγ (Th1) or IL-17 production (Th17) following P. copri colonization.
source: although no statistically significant differences were seen in IFNγ (Th1) or IL-17 production (Th17) following P. copri colonization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry analysis of lamina propria T cells.

claim: No differences in Foxp3+ CD4+ T-cells were observed following P. copri colonization.
source: Likewise, no differences in Foxp3+ CD4+ T-cells were observed.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry analysis of lamina propria T cells.

claim: A Prevotella-defined microbiome may have the propensity to support inflammation in the context of a genetically susceptible host.
source: These data suggest that a Prevotella-defined microbiome may have the propensity to support inflammation in the context of a genetically susceptible host.
evidence: This is an inference from the mouse colitis data.

claim: RA occurs in sequential phases.
source: Multiple lines of investigation have revealed that RA is a multifactorial disease that occurs in sequential phases.
evidence: This is established knowledge from RA research.

claim: There is a prolonged period of autoimmunity in a pre-clinical state that lasts many years before clinical RA.
source: Notably, there is a prolonged period of autoimmunity (i.e., presence of circulating auto-antibodies such as rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies) in a pre-clinical state that lasts many years, during which time there is no clinical or histologic evidence of inflammatory arthritis (Deane et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Before the onset of clinical disease, there is an increase in autoantibody titers and epitope spreading coupled with elevation in circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Before the onset of clinical disease, there is an increase in autoantibody titers and epitope spreading coupled with elevation in circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is established knowledge from RA research.

claim: These findings have led to the 'second-event' hypothesis in RA, which proposes that an environmental factor triggers systemic joint inflammation in the context of pre-existent autoimmunity.
source: These findings have led to the 'second-event' hypothesis in RA, which proposes that an environmental factor triggers systemic joint inflammation in the context of pre-existent autoimmunity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis in the field based on clinical observations.

claim: Multiple mucosal sites and their residing microbial communities have been implicated in RA, including the airways, the periodontal tissue and the intestinal lamina propria.
source: Multiple mucosal sites and their residing microbial communities have been implicated, including the airways, the periodontal tissue and the intestinal lamina propria (Mcinnes and Schett, 2011; Scher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on cited reviews of the field.

claim: A role for the gut microbiota has been clearly established in animal models of arthritis.
source: Although a role for the gut microbiota has been clearly established in animal models of arthritis
evidence: This is established knowledge from animal model studies.

claim: It is not known if dysbiosis influences human RA.
source: it is not known if dysbiosis influences human RA
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The human gut microbiota has been classified into unique enterotypes, one of which is defined by the predominance of Prevotella.
source: The human gut microbiota has been classified into unique enterotypes, one of which is defined by the predominance of Prevotella (Arumugam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: The microbiota of many subjects in the cohort was defined by a single taxon—P. copri—which was associated with the majority of untreated, new-onset rheumatoid arthritis (NORA) patients.
source: In our cohort, we found the microbiota of many subjects to be defined by a single taxon—P. copri—which was associated with the majority of untreated, new-onset rheumatoid arthritis (NORA) patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: P. copri was detected in a minority of healthy subjects in cohorts from the Human Microbiome Project, the European MetaHIT project, and this study.
source: P. copri was also detected in a minority of healthy subjects in cohorts from the Human Microbiome Project (Human Microbiome Project Consortium, 2012), the European MetaHIT project (Qin et al., 2010), and our study.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data from this study and cited projects.

claim: The prevalence of P. copri in chronic rheumatoid arthritis (CRA) patients was similar to that observed in the healthy subjects.
source: Surprisingly, the prevalence of P. copri in chronic rheumatoid arthritis (CRA) patients, all of whom had been treated and exhibited reduced disease activity, was similar to that observed in the healthy subjects.
evidence: This is based on analysis of P. copri prevalence data.

claim: One hypothesis is that the Prevotella-defined microbiota fail to thrive when there is less inflammation, perhaps due to a lack of inflammation-derived terminal electron acceptors.
source: One hypothesis is that the Prevotella-defined microbiota fail to thrive when there is less inflammation, perhaps due to a lack of inflammation-derived terminal electron acceptors, as seen for E. coli in inflammatory bowel disease (Winter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors, with reference to a cited study.

claim: The gut microbiota changes observed in newly diagnosed RA patients may be the consequence of a unique, NORA-specific systemic inflammatory response.
source: Alternatively, the gut microbiota changes observed in newly diagnosed RA patients may be the consequence of a unique, NORA-specific systemic inflammatory response.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: DAS28 scores were slightly lower in CRA and PsA patients compared to NORA.
source: While DAS28 scores were slightly lower in CRA and PsA patients (Table 1)
evidence: This is based on clinical data from the study cohorts.

claim: The most remarkable difference between NORA and other patient groups was in levels of C-reactive protein (CRP).
source: the most remarkable difference was in levels of C-reactive protein (CRP)
evidence: This is based on clinical data from the study cohorts.

claim: CRP may have microbial modulating properties.
source: This raises the question of whether CRP itself may have microbial modulating properties.
evidence: This is a speculative question raised by the authors.

claim: CRP is characteristically high in early and flaring RA, but not in other autoimmune diseases.
source: CRP is characteristically high in early and flaring RA, but not in other autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematous, scleroderma, and PsA).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: CRP is a member of the pentraxin protein family.
source: A member of the pentraxin protein family, CRP was first identified in the plasma of patients with Streptococcus pneumoniae infection (Tillett and Francis, 1930).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited historical study.

claim: The primary bacterial ligand for CRP is phosphocholine, a component of multiple bacterial cell-wall components, including lipopolysaccharides (LPS).
source: Further, the primary bacterial ligand for CRP is phosphocholine, a component of multiple bacterial cell-wall components, including lipopolysaccharides (LPS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRP biochemistry.

claim: CRP binding to bacterial phosphocholine activates the complement system and enhances phagocytosis by macrophages.
source: CRP binding to bacterial phosphocholine activates the complement system and enhances phagocytosis by macrophages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRP function.

claim: Whether or not CRP itself represents a specific response to the presence of P. copri in NORA is an area of future investigation.
source: Whether or not CRP itself represents a specific response to the presence of P. copri in NORA is an area of future investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Prevotella-dominated healthy omnivore individuals were recently reported to have increased basal levels of serum TMAO compared to Bacteroides-dominated healthy individuals.
source: Interestingly, Prevotella-dominated healthy omnivore individuals were recently reported to have increased basal levels of serum TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide), a product of inflammation linked to atherogenesis, compared to Bacteroides-dominated healthy individuals (Koeth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: TMAO could be derived from increased consumption of meat.
source: While TMAO could be derived from increased consumption of meat (Koeth et al., 2013)
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Prevotella has been previously associated with a dearth of meat in the diet.
source: Prevotella has been previously associated with a dearth of meat in the diet (Wu et al., 2011)
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Additional studies are needed to determine if prevalence of P. copri in the microbiota is associated with changes in specific metabolites.
source: Additional studies are needed to determine if prevalence of P. copri in the microbiota is associated with changes in specific metabolites.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Sequence alignment most closely linked NORA-associated Prevotella with the P. copri genome.
source: Sequence alignment most closely linked NORA-associated Prevotella with the P. copri genome.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Large regions of the P. copri genome were scarcely covered in both the study cohort and subjects of the HMP.
source: Interestingly, large regions of the P. copri genome were scarcely covered in both our cohort and subjects of the HMP.
evidence: This is based on genome coverage analysis.

claim: Differences in P. copri genome coverage may reflect geographically-associated strain variability.
source: As the reference strain of P. copri was isolated in Japan and all samples analyzed in our study were collected and sequenced in North America, these differences may reflect geographically-associated strain variability, consistent with a report ranking P. copri as the second-most variable member of the human gut microbiota between continents (Schloissnig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on geographic differences and a cited study.

claim: Comparison of sequences in NORA samples with those of P. copri-dominated healthy individuals evaluated in the HMP allowed identification of ORFs associated with the NORA phenotype.
source: Notably, comparison of sequences in NORA samples with those of P. copri-dominated healthy individuals evaluated in the HMP allowed us to identify ORFs associated with the NORA phenotype.
evidence: This is based on comparative metagenomic analysis.

claim: Two ORFs encoding components of an iron transporter were specific for NORA-associated P. copri.
source: Two ORFs, both encoding components of an iron transporter, were specific for NORA-associated P. copri
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ORF presence/absence.

claim: Two ORFs encoding components of a nuo operon were specific for HLT-associated P. copri.
source: while two ORFs were specific for HLT-associated P. copri and encode components of a nuo operon
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ORF presence/absence.

claim: Iron transporters are known to be virulence factors in other bacterial clades.
source: Iron transporters are known to be virulence factors in other bacterial clades
evidence: This is established knowledge from microbiology.

claim: The ubiquinone oxidoreductase pathway encoded by the nuo operon may provide a fitness advantage in the context of a healthy microbiome by allowing use of metabolites available therein.
source: while the ubiquinone oxidoreductase pathway encoded by the nuo operon may provide a fitness advantage in the context of a healthy microbiome by allowing use of metabolites available therein
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional significance of the nuo operon.

claim: Colonization with P. copri increases the pre-test probability of NORA from 1% to approximately 3.95% in western cohorts.
source: While colonization with P. copri increases the pre-test probability of NORA from 1% to approximately 3.95% in western cohorts (by Bayes' theorem, see 'Materials and methods')
evidence: This is based on Bayesian statistical calculation using prevalence data.

claim: The presence of one of the NORA-specific ORFs may markedly increase the pre-test probability of NORA status.
source: the presence of one of the aforementioned ORFs may markedly increase the pre-test probability of NORA status
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the diagnostic potential of the identified ORFs.

claim: The diagnostic application of these biomarkers needs to be confirmed in larger cohorts.
source: The diagnostic application of these biomarkers needs to be confirmed in larger cohorts.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Analysis of enzymatic functions in the Prevotella-dominated metagenome reveals a significant decrease in purine metabolic pathways, including tetrahydrofolate (THF) biosynthesis.
source: Analysis of enzymatic functions in the Prevotella-dominated metagenome reveals a significant decrease in purine metabolic pathways, including tetrahydrofolate (THF) biosynthesis.
evidence: This is based on HUMAnN functional metagenomic analysis.

claim: This may have therapeutic implications since methotrexate (MTX), a folate analogue and a dihydrofolate (DHF) reductase inhibitor, remains the anchor drug for the treatment of RA.
source: This may have therapeutic implications since methotrexate (MTX), a folate analogue and a dihydrofolate (DHF) reductase inhibitor, remains the anchor drug for the treatment of RA (Singh et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a speculative inference about therapeutic implications, with reference to a cited study.

claim: MTX has inter-individual variability in terms of absorption and bioavailability.
source: and has inter-individual variability in terms of absorption and bioavailability
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: The THF biosynthetic pathway encoded by the gut metagenome may compete with host DHF reductase for MTX binding and metabolism.
source: The THF biosynthetic pathway encoded by the gut metagenome, which includes a DHF reductase enzyme, may compete with host DHF reductase for MTX binding and metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about MTX metabolism.

claim: An increase in DHF reductase-high microbiota in some RA subjects may help explain why only about half of RA patients respond adequately to oral MTX.
source: If so, an increase in DHF reductase-high microbiota in some RA subjects (i.e., Bacteroides overabundant) may help explain, at least partially, why only about half of RA patients respond adequately to oral MTX, ultimately requiring either parenteral administration or the addition of complementary immunosuppressants.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting microbiome composition to MTX response.

claim: Prevotella-high NORA subjects, with a dearth of DHF reductase in the gut, may respond better to oral MTX.
source: Prevotella-high NORA subjects, with a dearth of DHF reductase in the gut, may respond better to oral MTX.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about MTX response in Prevotella-high subjects.

claim: Prospective human studies should help to clarify these observations about MTX response and microbiome composition.
source: Prospective human studies should help to clarify these observations.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: A recently published study with HLA-DR transgenic mice revealed that the gut microbiota was, at least partially, regulated by the HLA genes.
source: A recently published study with HLA-DR transgenic mice revealed that the gut microbiota was, at least partially, regulated by the HLA genes (Gomez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Arthritis-susceptible DRB1*04:01 transgenic mice had a markedly different intestinal microbiota when compared to arthritis-resistant DRB1*04:02 animals.
source: Arthritis-susceptible DRB1*04:01 transgenic mice had a markedly different intestinal microbiota when compared to arthritis-resistant DRB1*04:02 animals
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: The difference in intestinal microbiota between DRB1*04:01 and DRB1*04:02 mice was associated with altered mucosal immune function and increased intestinal permeability.
source: and this was associated with altered mucosal immune function (i.e., increased gene transcripts for Th17-related cytokines) and increased intestinal permeability
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: SE risk-alleles in humans may have an impact on the composition of the gut microbiota.
source: Our results suggest that, similarly, SE risk-alleles in humans may have an impact on the composition of the gut microbiota.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings on SE alleles and P. copri abundance.

claim: Patients in the NORA cohort showed a significant inverse correlation between P. copri relative abundance and presence of SE alleles.
source: Intriguingly, patients in the NORA cohort showed a significant inverse correlation between P. copri relative abundance and presence of SE alleles (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of P. copri abundance and SE allele status.

claim: Certain human gut microbial communities may be determined by specific MHC alleles that favor the expansion of particular species.
source: It is therefore possible that, as in mice, certain human gut microbial communities are determined by specific MHC alleles that favor the expansion of particular species.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the mouse data and human findings.

claim: This could represent a gene-environment interaction that contributes to RA pathogenesis.
source: As in the case of cigarette smoking, this could also represent a gene-environment interaction that contributes to RA pathogenesis.

claim: A certain threshold for P. copri abundance may be necessary to overcome the lack of genetic predisposition in RA subjects.
source: It is conceivable that a certain threshold for P. copri abundance may be necessary to overcome the lack of genetic predisposition in RA subjects

claim: A lower P. copri abundance may be sufficient to trigger disease in those carrying risk-alleles.
source: while a lower abundance may be sufficient to trigger disease in those carrying risk-alleles
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the relationship between P. copri abundance and genetic risk.

source: Colonization of mice with P. copri recapitulated the differences in relative abundances of Prevotella and Bacteroides previously reported in humans

source: and confirmed the ability of P. copri to dominate the colonic commensal microbiota in the absence of apparent disease (Faust et al., 2012)

claim: The shift in abundances correlated with a metagenomic shift, which may support and/or perpetuate an inflammatory environment.
source: This shift in abundances correlated with a metagenomic shift, which may support and/or perpetuate an inflammatory environment.

source: For example, uniquely present superoxide reductase in P. copri may facilitate resistance to or allow the use of host-derived reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated during inflammation, perhaps as terminal electron acceptors for respiration (Winter et al., 2013).

source: Similarly, the P. copri genome encodes phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase (PAPS), an oxidoreductase absent in Bacteroides that participates in sulfur metabolism and leads to the production of thioredoxin.

source: An appealing hypothesis from an evolutionary and ecological perspective is that the P. copri-defined microbiota thrives in a pro-inflammatory environment and may exacerbate inflammation for its own benefit.

source: Another key feature of the P. copri-dominated microbiome is a community shift away from Bacteroides, Group XIV Clostridia, Blautia, and Lachnospiraceae clades
evidence: This is based on analysis of the microbiome data.

source: previously reported to be associated with an anti-inflammatory state and regulatory T-cell (Treg) production (Atarashi et al., 2011; Round et al., 2011)

evidence: This is a speculative inference with reference to a cited study.

source: Further characterization of changes in the host immune system associated with a Prevotella-dominated microbiota should provide deeper insight into whether expansion of P. copri contributes causally to the development of autoimmunity in early onset RA.
